text: Before police force their way into your home, they knock and announce. In 2006 the Supreme Court decided what happens when they do not.
provenance: Before police force their way into a home, they knock, they announce who they are, and they give you a moment to reach the door.

text: Detroit, 1998. Police hold a valid warrant. They announce themselves, then wait three to five seconds before going through an unlocked door. The violation is admitted.
provenance: Police hold a valid warrant to search the home of a man named Booker Hudson.

and then they wait only three to five seconds before going through an unlocked door. It is not long enough. Everyone in the case agrees it is not long enough; Michigan does not even argue the point. The violation is admitted.

text: The Court answers five to four. The rule is still a command of the Fourth Amendment. Police still have to obey it. What it takes away is the punishment.
provenance: The knock-and-announce rule, he writes, is still a command of the Fourth Amendment. It still exists. Police still have to obey it. The Court does not say officers can stop knocking.
What the Court takes away is the punishment.

text: The dissent is blunt. Take away the remedy, and you take away the rule. A right with no consequence for breaking it is not really a right.
provenance: Take away the remedy, he says, and you take away the rule.
A right with no consequence for breaking it, he writes, is not really a right at all.

text: What is left is a civil lawsuit you bring yourself, years after the door is already off its hinges. The knocking rule is still there.
provenance: The majority's reply is that one remedy still stands — a civil lawsuit.
